paragraphs: A company wanted to build a very big technology park in Kilmeaden. Kilmeaden is a small village near Waterford city. Now the plan has been refused.
The park was going to have data centres. Data centres are buildings full of computers. They use a lot of electricity and water. The plan also had a café, a shop and a childcare centre.
The planners said no. They were worried about more traffic. They were also worried about water and electricity.
More than 500 people did not want the park. About 300 people live in the village.
Some politicians now want to stop new data centres that do not use clean energy. They say families pay for this energy in their bills.
Some politicians and campaigners want the Government to stop new data centres that do not use clean energy. They spoke after a plan for a big development in Kilmeaden, Co Waterford, was refused.

The technology park was planned for a site about 12 kilometres from Waterford city. It would have been larger than one square kilometre. Besides data centres, it was going to include a new village centre with a café, a shop, a pharmacy, a gym and a childcare building. The Irish company Echelon was behind the plan.

Planners refused permission because of more traffic and extra pressure on water and electricity. More than 500 people objected. Many said the project would change the small village, which has about 300 people, too much.

Roderic O'Gorman, a Green Party TD, said there should again be a ban on data centres that use fossil fuels. The current government ended the last ban. He said ordinary families pay for the energy of data centres through their bills.
David Cullinane of Sinn Féin said Ireland needs a clear national plan for data centres.
Politicians and campaigners have called for a pause on new data centres that cannot run on renewable energy, after planning permission was refused for a large development in Kilmeaden, Co Waterford.

The proposed technology park, about 12 kilometres from Waterford city, would have covered more than one square kilometre. As well as data centres, the plans included a new village centre with a café, shop, pharmacy and gym, and a childcare facility. The Irish company behind it, Echelon, has leased data centres to firms such as TikTok.

Permission was refused because of expected increases in traffic and the extra pressure the campus would put on water and electricity supplies. More than 500 people had objected, and critics said it would completely change the village, where about 300 people live.

Green Party TD Roderic O'Gorman said the ban on data centres that rely on fossil fuels should return. The previous moratorium was lifted by the current government. He argued that households end up paying for the energy that data centres use.
Sinn Féin TD David Cullinane called for a national approach that takes account of electricity demand, climate targets and the impact on local communities.

Campaigners and politicians are clamouring for a moratorium on data centres that cannot be powered by renewable energy, in the wake of a planning refusal for a sprawling development in Kilmeaden, Co Waterford.

The proposed technology campus, some 12 kilometres outside Waterford city, would have spanned more than a square kilometre. Alongside the data halls, the blueprint envisaged a new village centre complete with a café, shop, pharmacy and gym, as well as a childcare facility. The developer, the Irish firm Echelon, counts TikTok among its tenants.

Permission was turned down on the grounds of projected traffic growth and the strain the scheme would place on water and electricity supplies. Upwards of 500 objections were lodged, with opponents warning that the village, home to roughly 300 people, would be transformed beyond recognition.

Green Party TD Roderic O'Gorman urged the reinstatement of the moratorium scrapped by the current government, contending that households ultimately foot the bill for the power such facilities consume.
Sinn Féin TD David Cullinane, meanwhile, called for a coherent national strategy that weighs electricity demand and climate obligations against the toll on local communities.
